title: Particle model & density
examples: How do particles move in a gas?
What is the difference between liquid and gas particles?
Can you show me the particle arrangement in solids?

explain.say: Today we are looking at the particle model of matter.
Now let me show you the real thing in 3D: solid, liquid and gas. Look at the solid, the liquid and the gas. Tap any part, and I will tell you what it does.
We learn that matter exists in different states.
In solids, particles are packed closely together.
Liquids have particles that can slide past one another.

draw.text: Liquid: Particles slide past each other

explain.say: Gases have particles that move randomly and quickly.
When gas particles hit the container walls, they push outwards.

faq.q: Why do gases push on the walls of their container?
faq.a: Gas pressure is caused by the particles hitting the container walls. These collisions transfer momentum, which we measure as pressure.
asks: How does particle motion create pressure?

faq.q: Are the particles in a liquid always touching each other?
faq.a: No, in a liquid, particles are close but they can slide past each other. They are not locked into place like in a solid.
asks: How is a liquid different from a solid?

faq.q: Does the temperature affect the particle movement?
faq.a: Yes, increasing the temperature increases the average kinetic energy of the particles. This makes them move faster.
asks: What happens to particles when it gets hot?
How is temperature related to particle speed?

faq.q: If I compress a gas, what happens to the pressure?
faq.a: Compressing a gas forces the particles closer together. This increases the frequency of collisions, thus increasing the pressure.
asks: Does squeezing a gas change its pressure?
What happens to collision rate when volume decreases?

faq.q: Is the density of a gas always low?
faq.a: Generally, yes, because the particles are far apart. Density measures mass per unit volume, and gases have very little mass in a large volume.
asks: How does particle spacing affect density?
Are gases always less dense than solids?

facts: In solids, particles vibrate about fixed positions.
In gases, particles move randomly and rapidly.
Gas pressure results from particle collisions with container walls.
Temperature is related to the average kinetic energy of particles.

quiz.say: Which state has particles that vibrate in fixed positions?
quiz.why: Particles in a solid are held in fixed positions, only vibrating slightly.

wrong.0: Plasma is a state not covered in this basic model.
wrong.2: Liquids can flow and change shape, meaning particles are not fixed.
wrong.3: Gases move very quickly and randomly, not in fixed spots.

quiz.say: If you increase the temperature of a gas, what happens to its particles?
quiz.why: Higher temperature means more energy, causing particles to move with greater speed.

wrong.1: Temperature change affects speed, not necessarily the packing density.
wrong.2: Stopping movement would mean zero temperature, which is absolute zero.
wrong.3: Changing state requires more than just increasing temperature.

quiz.say: If you squeeze a gas into a smaller box, the pressure increases because:

options.show: The container walls push back harder
options.say: The container walls push back harder

quiz.why: Fewer spaces mean particles hit the walls more often, increasing the force.

wrong.0: The pressure increase comes from the particles hitting the walls, not the walls pushing back.
wrong.2: Compression usually keeps the energy high, so speed does not decrease.
wrong.3: Compression alone does not change the state to solid.
